div.head: Introduction
div.p: Our living and working environments are now full of real-time digital controllers and autonomous devices. Many autonomous devices have high stability requirements, in the sense that outputs must be produced in regular or predictable intervals so as to meet safety concerns and to provide smooth operations. This is important for real-time systems like those used t o handle sensitive chemical ingredients, or synchronized audio and video sources (as in multimedia systems). Unpredictable output timings, or jatters, are undesirable in these applications [8, 91. One way to ensure jitterless outputs is to make sure that the temporal distance between any two consecutive executions of a task stream is always less than a well-defined time interval. For example, a video system needs to ensure that the inter-arrival time between video frames is always less than 33 ms. Such systems are called Distance-Constrained Task System (DCTS) [4]. DCTS is different from the periodic task model 1052-8725/96 $5.00 0 1996 IEEE [ll] that requires at least one task completion in every period, which allows for an inter-completion time of greater than the period length. In fact, the intercompletion interval of a periodic task could be as long as twice the period minus the task execution time.

Pinwheel algorithms [4,7,91 have been shown to provide satisfactory DCTS schedules. In addition to being used as a single processor scheduler, algorithms for distributed pinwheel scheduling [7] and network scheduling [3] have also been presented. All these schedulers have well-defined and simple schedulability conditions so that it is easy for a system to check if all tasks can be successfully scheduled. This is important if systems need to accept tasks that arrive dynamically at run time. The task schedule produced by the pinwheel schedulers that use the single-number reduction technique (to be discussed later) has a constant intercompletion time. This not only enhances the system predictability but also makes it easier to synchronize both intra-and inter-task computations.

Our research for the DCTS scheduling problem is based on the pinwheel scheduler Sr [4]. Sr uses a period specialization technique to transform all task distance constraints to multiples based on 2, e.g. {3,6, 12, 24). However, some distance constraints can be specialized to multiples based on other numbers, such as (3, 15,75} for base 5. In [9], a pinwheel scheduler Srb has been proposed so that all possible bases are tested in Sr to find the optimal base that minimizes the total density increase due to the specialization procedure. However, neither the schedulability condition nor the optimality proof of S r b was presented.
We continue the work in [9] and present a generalized Sr scheduler, called Sr9, that specializes distance constraints to multiples based on any integer g 2 2.
Based on Sr9, we study the schedulability condition for Sr'. The proof of optimality for Srb is presented. Since Srb has an exponential time complexity, we also ]It was denoted as Srb.
design a heuristic algorithm HSr to find a suboptimal solution in polynomial time. In our simulation, we find that the performance of HSr is almost as good as Srb.

The contribution of this paper is that we have investigated and designed the optimal scheduler in the class of pinwheel schedulers using the single-number reduction technique. This is useful for practical systems with distance constraints (or periods) that are not multiples based on 2. We have derived the schedulability conditions for different bases and also studied the behavior of near-optimal algorithms. The paper therefore provides important results both theoretically and practically.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the background on pinwheel schedulers and Sr. Section 3 discusses Scheduler Srg and its schedulability condition. The scheduler Srb and its schedulability condition are presented in Section 4. We show its optimality property. We also study the performance of a heuristic scheduler HSr by simulation. The paper is concluded in Section 5.

Another potential benefit of adopting the pinwheel model is that system schedules can be produced in polynomial time [6]. Therefore, task schedules can be produced at run time when tasks arrive dynamically. The schedules produced can be used to reserve the ex- ecution time for some highly time-critical tasks. Tasks with less criticality may use the remaining time to execute, and even use different scheduling policies. In this way, it will be feasible for the system to mix different schedule policies to achieve the best predictability as well as schedulability.

div.head: Performance study
div.p: We have studied the performances of Srb and HSr by simulation. In our simulation, the number of tasks ranges from 2 to 20 and the original density ranges from 70% to 100%. We randomly generated 10000 task sets (uniformly distributed) for each case and compared the density increase and percentage of schedulability with that of using Sr.

In the following we show the simulation result for Sr, Sr <3 (Srb using only bases 2 and 3), Sr <IO ( S r b using only bases less than lo), Sr < l o o (Srb using only bases less than loo), HSr, and srb. From our simulation result, we find that the schedulability percentage of HSr is the same as Srb.

Figure 3 shows the differences of total densities after task sets are specialized by Sr and by Srb. Figure 3(a) shows the average difference for the task sets which are schedulable by Sr and Figure 3(b) shows the average difference for all schedulable task sets. Figure 3(a) has decreasing values when the total utilization for the task set is greater than the schedulability bound of Sr. However, if we include those cases unschedulable by Sr but schedulable by Srb, the average difference increases dramatically. We find the improvement of using S r b for the task sets with higher original utilization is subst antial.

Figure 4(a) shows the difference on the percentages of schedulable tasks using Sr and using Srb. Among those schedulable by S r b , Figure 4(b) shows the percentage of those also schedulable by Sr. Figures 5,6 and 7 show similar comparisons as in Figure 4 except we compare Srb with Sr 53, Sr 110 and Sr 5100 respectively. We can see for the task sets with an original density less than 0.9, Sr < 3 can schedule about 90% of the tasks schedulable by Srb, and with original density less than 0.95, Sr 510 can schedule about 92% of tasks schedulable by Srb. For Sr <loo in Figure 7, it performs almost as good as Srb. In other words, trying any base larger than 100 will not improve the schedulable percentage.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, a generalized pinwheel scheduler Srg which is based on Sr is presented. The schedulability condition for Srg has been derived. It is shown that using Srbl which tries all possible bases, a system has a better chance to find a good specialization result than Sr. Srb is proved to be the optimal pinwheel algorithm using the single-number reduction technique. We have also presented a heuristic algorithm HSr and compared its performance to Srb. From the simulation, we can see that both HSr and Sr <loo has almost the same schedulable percentage as S g . However, the actual computation cost of HSr is lower than Sr <loo. Therefore, we believe that HSr is the most practical algorithm for single-node pinwheel scheduling.
